nodes.label: The Ubaid culture of southern Mesopotamia
nodes.full: The Ubaid culture flourishes in the river-valley towns of southern Mesopotamia through this whole period — the source of the painted pottery, the maritime contact, and eventually the herding and boat technology reaching the Arabian shore.
nodes.src: background; Carter, "The Ubaid and the Gulf" (2010)

nodes.label: Marawah island — the earliest stone architecture in Arabia
nodes.full: Multi-room drystone houses on Marawah are the oldest built structures yet found in the UAE and among the oldest in the Arabian Peninsula — a shift from mobile foraging to anchored coastal communities living off fish, shellfish and small herds.

nodes.label: Dalma island community — dates, pottery and Gulf-wide contact
nodes.full: A settled community on Dalma left plastered floors, Ubaid-type painted sherds carried from Mesopotamia, and charred date stones — some of the earliest evidence anywhere for people eating dates.

nodes.label: Jebel al-Buhais — an inland herding society and its cemetery
nodes.full: At the desert-edge spring of al-Buhais, a community herding domestic sheep, goat and cattle buried its dead in a large collective cemetery over centuries — the fullest picture of an inland Arabian Neolithic society yet excavated.

nodes.label: As-Sabiyah — an Ubaid-linked settlement on Kuwait Bay
nodes.full: The H3 site on Kuwait Bay yielded Ubaid pottery, a painted ceramic boat model and bitumen slabs bearing barnacle and reed impressions — traces of reed boats caulked with Mesopotamian bitumen.

nodes.label: The 'Dark Millennium' — settlement retreat
nodes.full: As the monsoon withdrew and the interior dried, dated sites across eastern Arabia thin out sharply for roughly eight centuries. Populations contracted onto the coast and a few springs.

nodes.label: Hafit horizon begins — cairn tombs and the first oasis villages
nodes.full: Beehive cairn tombs strung along the ridges of Jebel Hafit, and the earliest mud-brick at Hili and Bat, mark the resettlement of the interior at the very end of this folio's span.
nodes.src: Frifelt, "The Island of Umm an-Nar" vol.1

nodes.label: Projectile injuries in the al-Buhais cemetery
nodes.full: A minority of the al-Buhais dead show healed or perimortem trauma, including flint arrow tips lodged in bone — occasional lethal violence between individuals or small groups, not organised warfare.

nodes.label: Contested access to springs and wells
nodes.full: As surface water failed during the arid hiatus, the few permanent springs and hand-dug wells became chokepoints. Clustered burials and repeated reoccupation of the same water sources suggest kin groups asserting durable claims over them.

nodes.label: The collective cemetery as a claim on place
nodes.full: Hundreds of individuals of both sexes and all ages were buried together at al-Buhais over many generations, with grave goods distributed fairly evenly — a cemetery reused this long is itself an institution marking the group's territory.

nodes.label: Desert 'kites' — cooperative hunting architecture
nodes.full: Long low stone walls funnelling gazelle and oryx into killing enclosures required many hands to build and to work — the clearest prehistoric evidence in Arabia of labour organised beyond the single household.

nodes.label: Ornament and animal offerings in Neolithic burials
nodes.full: Al-Buhais burials contain thousands of beads of shell, carnelian and mother-of-pearl, pierced pendants, and the bones of goats and gazelles placed with the dead — consistent treatment implying a shared body of belief about death.

nodes.label: The Akab dugong bone mound
nodes.full: On Akab, people stacked the skulls and bones of dozens of butchered dugongs into a deliberate mound, arranging skulls in rows and adding stone tools and beads — one of the earliest ritual monuments known from the Arabian coast.

nodes.label: Early rock art of the Hajar mountains
nodes.full: Pecked images of hunters, ibex, snakes and later camels cover rock faces across the Hajar range. The oldest panels — weathered hunting scenes beneath datable Bronze Age additions — likely reach back into this period.

nodes.label: The al-Buhais bead industry
nodes.full: Buhais artisans ground and drilled beads from Gulf shell, imported carnelian and soft stone, producing standardised forms in enormous quantity — bodily ornament as the signature craft of the inland Neolithic.

nodes.label: Ubaid painted pottery on the Arabian shore
nodes.full: Fine buff pottery painted with geometric bands in dark pigment — made in southern Mesopotamia — turns up at Neolithic sites the length of the Arabian coast. Local communities had no pottery of their own; these vessels were prestige imports.
nodes.src: Carter, in Carter & Philip (eds.), "Beyond the Ubaid" (2010)

nodes.label: The As-Sabiyah ceramic boat model
nodes.full: A small painted clay model of a high-prowed reed boat, found with bitumen boat fragments, is among the oldest representations of a watercraft anywhere.

nodes.label: Tidal and seasonal timing encoded in coastal sites
nodes.full: Fish-trap alignments, the seasonality of pearl-oyster and fish remains, and the scheduling of island occupation show communities working to a detailed calendar of tides, winds and fish runs.
nodes.src: Beech, "In the Land of the Ichthyophagi" (2004)

nodes.label: Selective procurement of flint and carnelian
nodes.full: Neolithic knappers travelled to specific outcrops for the best flint and returned repeatedly to the same carnelian sources, bypassing nearer but poorer stone — implying a shared, transmitted map of raw material sources.

nodes.label: The Neolithic herding package reaches Arabia
nodes.full: Domestic sheep, goat and cattle — none of them native to Arabia — appear together at inland sites in the sixth millennium BC, brought across from the Levant or via Mesopotamia.

nodes.label: The world's oldest pearl — Marawah, c.5800 BC
nodes.full: A natural pearl recovered from a Neolithic house floor on Marawah is the oldest known anywhere — Gulf communities were already diving for and valuing pearls eight thousand years ago, the start of a trade that defined the region until the 1930s.

nodes.label: Neolithic fishing and shellfish economies
nodes.full: Coastal middens metres deep in fish bone and shell, barbed hooks of pearl shell, and net weights show intensive, near-industrial exploitation of the sea. Tuna and jack were caught offshore; dugong and turtle in the shallows.

nodes.label: Early date-palm use on Dalma
nodes.full: Charred date stones from Dalma are among the earliest evidence for date consumption anywhere. The date — storable, sugar-rich, salt-tolerant — was already part of the Gulf diet before farming villages existed.

nodes.label: Aridification forces a coastal economy
nodes.full: When the monsoon rains withdrew, interior herding collapsed and surviving communities concentrated on the coast, living on fish, shellfish and mangrove resources — a pattern repeated in every later Arabian drought.

nodes.label: Reed boats caulked with bitumen
nodes.full: Slabs of bitumen from As-Sabiyah preserve the impressions of reed bundles on one face and barnacles on the other — the coated hulls of seagoing reed boats. Mesopotamian bitumen made Gulf-wide voyaging possible a millennium before the sail.

nodes.label: Drystone architecture at Marawah
nodes.full: The Marawah houses — coursed beachrock walls forming several connected rooms, with plastered surfaces — are the earliest substantial masonry in south-east Arabia and a template for the Bronze Age.

nodes.label: The Arabian bifacial point tradition
nodes.full: Neolithic Arabian knappers produced finely pressure-flaked, tanged and barbed arrowheads — the peninsula's most distinctive lithic technology and a marker used to trace Neolithic populations across the interior.

nodes.label: Standardised bead-drilling
nodes.full: Consistent perforation diameters across thousands of Buhais beads imply a shared drilling technique using stone or possibly copper-tipped bow drills — a repeatable, teachable craft process rather than ad hoc production.

nodes.label: The Ubaid maritime network, Kuwait to Qatar to the UAE
nodes.full: For a thousand years, southern Mesopotamian communities sent pottery, bitumen and beads down the Arabian coast by boat, receiving pearls, shell and possibly dried fish in return — the earliest sustained long-distance exchange system in the region.
nodes.src: Carter (2010); Oates, Davidson, Kamilli & McKerrell, Antiquity 51 (1977)

nodes.label: Herding, pottery use and boat-building spread south
nodes.full: Domestic animals, the habit of using fine painted pottery, and bitumen boat technology all entered eastern Arabia from the north within the same window — the Neolithic Gulf plugged into the wider Near Eastern world.

nodes.label: Gulf shell and pearl reach Mesopotamia
nodes.full: Mother-of-pearl inlay and marine shell in the earliest levels of southern Mesopotamian towns come from the Gulf — the exchange ran both ways, the resources moving north before the first cities.

nodes.label: Modern humans through Arabia — Jebel Faya, c.125,000 BP
nodes.full: Stone tools from the base of the Jebel Faya rock-shelter, dated to about 125,000 years ago, resemble East African toolkits and predate the classic 'northern route' out of Africa — the deep prehistory beneath everything else in this folio.
nodes.src: Armitage, Jasim, Marks, Parker et al., Science 331 (2011)

nodes.label: The Holocene Humid Period — 'Green Arabia'
nodes.full: A northward shift of the monsoon filled the interior with lakes, grassland and savanna fauna — hippo, wild cattle, ostrich. This green window is what let herders and hunters spread across a peninsula now among the driest places on Earth.

nodes.label: The Gulf basin floods to its modern shoreline
nodes.full: At the last glacial maximum the Gulf was largely dry, a river valley running to a shrunken sea near Hormuz. Post-glacial sea-level rise drowned it, reaching roughly today's coast by about 4000 BC.

nodes.label: The end of the humid phase and the mid-Holocene crisis
nodes.full: Around 4000 BC the monsoon retreated south, lakes dried and the interior became desert within a few centuries. The resulting settlement collapse resets Arabian prehistory.

nodes.label: Egalitarian burial at Jebel al-Buhais
nodes.full: Men, women, the elderly and infants at al-Buhais received broadly similar graves and grave goods, with no cluster of unusually rich burials — a society without marked hereditary rank.

nodes.label: Women's fishing toolkits at Ra's al-Hamra
nodes.full: At the RH-5 cemetery in Muscat, adult women were frequently buried with pearl-shell fish-hooks and net gear, men less consistently so — women likely did much of the inshore fishing and shell-working.

nodes.label: A cared-for individual in the Buhais population
nodes.full: Several al-Buhais skeletons show healed serious fractures and degenerative disease that would have limited mobility for years, yet these people survived to be buried with the rest — their survival depended on the group absorbing the cost of their care.
